message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical, Chemical, and Isotopic Properties**

| Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Weighted average of its naturally occurring isotopes. |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest of all elements. |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Energy to remove the single valence electron. |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) | Energy released when an electron is added. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | Extremely low; hydrogen is a gas at room temperature. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | Solidifies only at cryogenic temperatures. |
| **Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.08988 g cm⁻³ | Very light; lighter than air. |
| **Molar volume (ideal gas, 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Standard molar volume. |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas | Diatomic H₂ molecules. |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Energy required to break H₂ into two H atoms. |
| **Dipole moment** | 0 D (non‑polar) | H₂ is a homonuclear diatomic molecule. |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series | Characteristic UV/visible/IR emission lines. |
| **Isotopes** |  |  |
| • **Protium (¹H)** | 1 proton, 0 neutrons | ~99.98 % natural abundance. |
| • **Deuterium (²H or D)** | 1 proton, 1 neutron | ~0.015 % natural abundance; heavier, used in nuclear fusion research. |
| • **Tritium (³H or T)** | 1 proton, 2 neutrons | Radioactive (half‑life ≈ 12.32 y); used in nuclear weapons and fusion experiments. |
| **Chemical behavior** |  |  |
| • **Oxidation states** | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (H₂) | Forms hydrides with metals, acids with non‑metals. |
| • **Acidity** | Strong acid (H⁺) | In aqueous solution, H⁺ is solvated as H₃O⁺. |
| • **Basicity** | Weak base (H⁻) | Hydride ion (H⁻) is a strong base. |
| • **Reactivity** | Highly reactive with oxygen, halogens, and many metals | Combustion produces water: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. |
| • **Combustion heat** | 286 kJ mol⁻¹ (per mole of H₂) | Energy released when hydrogen burns in oxygen. |
| **Physical uses** |  |  |
| • **Fuel** | Clean combustion (water vapor only) | Used in fuel cells, rockets, and potential hydrogen economy. |
| • **Industrial** | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, and other chemicals | Hydrogen is a key feedstock. |
| • **Cryogenics** | Cooling to very low temperatures | Liquid hydrogen used in space launch vehicles. |
| **Astrophysical role** |  |  |
| • **Stellar fusion** | Proton–proton chain, CNO cycle | Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium in stars. |
| • **Cosmological abundance** | ~75 % of baryonic mass | Most abundant element in the universe. |
| **Safety considerations** |  |  |
| • **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; wide flammability range (4–75 % H₂ in air) | Requires careful handling. |
| • **Explosive limits** | Lower explosive limit (LEL) 4 %, upper explosive limit (UEL) 75 % | At higher concentrations, hydrogen is inert. |
| • **Toxicity** | Non‑toxic but can displace oxygen, leading to asphyxiation | Ventilation is essential. |

---

### Quick Reference Summary

- **Atomic number:** 1  
- **Molecular form at STP:** H₂ (diatomic gas)  
- **Boiling point:** –252.9 °C (20 K)  
- **Density:** 0.0899 g cm⁻³  
- **Electronegativity:** 2.20  
- **Ionization energy:** 13.6 eV  
- **Isotopes:** ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium)  
- **Common oxidation states:** +1 (acidic), –1 (hydride), 0 (neutral H₂)  
- **Key reactions:** Combustion → H₂O; Fusion → He + energy  

Hydrogen’s unique combination of low mass, high reactivity, and abundance makes it central to chemistry, industry, energy technology, and astrophysics.
